concepts.title: net/http Fundamentals: Handlers and Routing
concepts.description: The entire net/http server story rests on one tiny interface, http.Handler, and one adapter type, http.HandlerFunc, that lets an ordinary function satisfy it -- understanding both, plus how http.ServeMux matches a request to a handler, is what everything else in building an HTTP service in Go is built on top of.
learningObjectives: Explain the http.Handler interface's single method and what ServeHTTP(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) is responsible for doing.
Explain what http.HandlerFunc is and why it lets an ordinary function value satisfy the Handler interface without defining a new named type.
Register routes on an http.ServeMux and start a server with http.ListenAndServe, and explain the role of http.DefaultServeMux.
Use Go 1.22+ enhanced ServeMux patterns (HTTP method prefixes and {wildcard} path segments) to route requests without a third-party router.
Explain why calling w.Write before setting a header, or calling w.WriteHeader more than once, produces bugs that don't show up as compile errors.

sections.heading: http.Handler: One Method, the Same Philosophy as io.Reader
http.HandlerFunc: Adapting a Plain Function Into a Handler
sections.body:
Defining a whole named struct type with a `ServeHTTP` method, as above, is overkill for a handler that's just one function with no state of its own. `http.HandlerFunc` is a small adapter type that solves this:

```go
type HandlerFunc func(ResponseWriter, *Request)

func (f HandlerFunc) ServeHTTP(w ResponseWriter, r *Request) {
	f(w, r)
}
```

`HandlerFunc` is a **named function type**. Any function with the signature `func(http.ResponseWriter, *http.Request)` can be converted to it, and the converted value has a `ServeHTTP` method (defined in the standard library) that calls the underlying function. That is what lets you write handlers as plain functions:

```go
func helloHandler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	fmt.Fprintln(w, "Hello from a plain function!")
}

http.Handle("/hello", http.HandlerFunc(helloHandler))   // explicit conversion, then it satisfies Handler
```

Note the conversion, `http.HandlerFunc(helloHandler)`: a bare function value `helloHandler` does **not** have a `ServeHTTP` method; only the converted `HandlerFunc` value does. In practice you'll more often see `http.HandleFunc("/hello", helloHandler)` (`HandleFunc`, not `Handle`), which does this conversion for you before registering the route. That is why it accepts a plain function while `http.Handle` requires something that's already an `http.Handler`.

sections.heading: Routing With ServeMux, and Go 1.22's Method and Wildcard Patterns
sections.body:
An `http.ServeMux` is an HTTP request multiplexer: you register patterns against handlers, and it picks the right handler for each incoming request based on the request's URL path (and, since Go 1.22, its method too):

```go
mux := http.NewServeMux()
mux.HandleFunc("/", homeHandler)
mux.HandleFunc("/about", aboutHandler)
http.ListenAndServe(":8080", mux)
```

`http.ListenAndServe(addr, handler)` starts a blocking TCP listener on `addr` and dispatches every incoming request to `handler`'s `ServeHTTP` method -- passing `nil` instead of an explicit mux uses `http.DefaultServeMux`, a single shared, package-level `ServeMux` that `http.HandleFunc` (the package-level function, not the method on your own mux) registers routes onto implicitly. The package-level default is fine for a quick script, but real services usually create their own `http.NewServeMux()`: a shared global mux lets unrelated packages (including third-party ones that register on `http.DefaultServeMux`) collide on route registration. A duplicate or conflicting pattern makes `Handle` panic at startup. `ListenAndServe` only returns when the server fails, so production code checks its error, usually as `log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(addr, mux))`; the short examples below leave that out.

**Go 1.22** upgraded what a `ServeMux` pattern can express, so many services no longer need a third-party router. Patterns can now be prefixed with an HTTP method, and path segments can contain named wildcards:

```go
// fragment: the first three lines belong inside main
mux := http.NewServeMux()
mux.HandleFunc("GET /users/{id}", getUserHandler)
mux.HandleFunc("DELETE /users/{id}", deleteUserHandler)

func getUserHandler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	id := r.PathValue("id")   // the actual path segment matched by {id}
	fmt.Fprintf(w, "fetching user %s", id)
}
```

`"GET /users/{id}"` matches only GET requests to a path shaped like `/users/anything` (and, by the 1.22 rules, HEAD). A DELETE to the same path goes to the separate `"DELETE /users/{id}"` registration, with no `if r.Method == "GET"` branching in either handler. `r.PathValue("id")` returns whatever the `{id}` segment matched for that request. Before Go 1.22, method-specific routing and path parameters meant inspecting `r.Method` and parsing `r.URL.Path` by hand, which is why many Go services reached for a third-party router such as gorilla/mux or chi. That need is much smaller now.

sections.heading: ResponseWriter: A Write-Once Status Line, and Why Order Matters

examples.title: A Struct-Based Handler and a Minimal Server
examples.explanation: `greeter` satisfies `http.Handler` by having a `ServeHTTP(http.ResponseWriter, *http.Request)` method; nothing declares that it implements `Handler`. The compiler checks this where `mux.Handle("/hello", greeter{...})` is called, since `Handle`'s second parameter is typed as `http.Handler`. Because `greeter` carries a `name` field, each instance can be configured differently (`greeter{name: "Gopher"}` here). A bare function would need a closure or package-level variable for that, and this is where a struct-based handler earns its extra verbosity over a plain `HandlerFunc`.

examples.title: HandlerFunc and the http.HandleFunc Convenience
examples.explanation: `helloHandler` is an ordinary function with no methods, so on its own it does not satisfy `http.Handler`. `mux.HandleFunc("/hello", helloHandler)` accepts the plain function and does the `http.HandlerFunc(helloHandler)` conversion before storing it, which is why `HandleFunc` exists alongside `Handle`. `Handle` needs something that is already an `http.Handler` (like the `greeter` struct in the previous example); `HandleFunc` does the wrapping. Most simple, stateless handlers are registered with `HandleFunc` rather than `mux.Handle("/hello", http.HandlerFunc(helloHandler))`.

examples.title: Go 1.22 Method-Specific and Wildcard Routing
examples.explanation: The two registrations share the path shape `/users/{id}` and differ only in the method prefix. They don't overlap: ServeMux sends a DELETE to the second handler and a GET to the first, and neither handler inspects `r.Method`. `r.PathValue("id")` returns the segment matched by `{id}`, so a request to `/users/42` gives `id == "42"` in whichever handler receives it. Before Go 1.22 the same routing needed a single handler on the `/users/` prefix that split `r.URL.Path` to extract the id and branched on `r.Method`.

misconceptions.description: Any function with the signature func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) automatically satisfies the http.Handler interface, with no conversion needed, the same way any type with a matching method automatically satisfies an interface.
misconceptions.clarification: Interface satisfaction in Go is based on methods, and a plain function has none, so it does not satisfy http.Handler, which requires a ServeHTTP method. What satisfies Handler is http.HandlerFunc, a named function type with that underlying signature, to which the standard library gives a ServeHTTP method that calls the function. Passing a plain function where an http.Handler is expected requires the conversion http.HandlerFunc(yourFunc), which costs nothing at run time because HandlerFunc is only a type conversion. The http.HandleFunc helper (and mux.HandleFunc) does that conversion for you.
misconceptions.fact: Interface satisfaction in Go is based on methods, not on bare function values -- a plain function of that signature has no methods at all, and therefore does not itself satisfy http.Handler, which requires a ServeHTTP method.

misconceptions.description: Calling w.WriteHeader(500) after the handler has already written some body content with w.Write or fmt.Fprintln will correctly change the status code the client receives to 500.
misconceptions.clarification: The status line and headers go to the client before any body bytes, so http.ResponseWriter locks in the status code the moment it is first determined: by an explicit WriteHeader call, or implicitly as 200 OK when the first Write happens without one. A later WriteHeader call has no effect on what the client receives; it only logs a 'superfluous response.WriteHeader call' warning on the server. Decide the final status code before writing any body content.

exercises.prompt: What HTTP status code does the client actually receive from this handler, and why, given that somethingWentWrong() returns true?
hints: The very first line calls fmt.Fprintln(w, ...), which writes body bytes through w.Write internally -- what does the FIRST Write call do if WriteHeader hasn't been explicitly called yet?
Once a status code is sent to the client -- explicitly or implicitly -- can a later WriteHeader call actually change it?
Trace exactly which line first sends the status line, and note that everything after that point is only adding to an already-committed response.
exercises.expectedAnswer: The client receives HTTP 200 OK, not 500. The first fmt.Fprintln call writes body bytes before any explicit WriteHeader call, which implicitly sends a 200 OK status immediately. The later w.WriteHeader(http.StatusInternalServerError) call has no effect on the already-sent status -- it only logs a 'superfluous WriteHeader call' warning on the server. The client sees a 200 response body containing both 'Report starting...' and 'An error occurred.'
exercises.solutionExplanation: `fmt.Fprintln(w, "Report starting...")` calls w.Write, and since no WriteHeader call has happened yet, Write sends `http.StatusOK` (200) before the body bytes. This happens on the first line, whether or not somethingWentWrong() later returns true. By the time the code reaches `w.WriteHeader(http.StatusInternalServerError)`, the status is already sent; the call does nothing for the client (apart from a server-side log warning), and 'An error occurred.' is appended to the body after the 200. The client gets a 200 OK whose body reads like an error, which misleads any caller that checks the status code instead of the text.

exercises.prompt: This route is meant to allow only GET requests to fetch an item by id, but a DELETE request to the same path unexpectedly also matches and runs the same handler, which was never written to check the method at all. Find and fix the bug.
hints: The registered pattern, "/items/{id}", has no HTTP method prefix at all -- what requests does a ServeMux pattern with no method prefix match?
Go 1.22+ ServeMux patterns can be prefixed with a specific HTTP method, like "GET /items/{id}", to restrict matching to only that method.

Add the "GET " prefix to the pattern so only GET requests reach this handler; a DELETE (or any other method) to the same path would then fall through to any other registered pattern, or to a 404/405 if none matches.
exercises.solutionExplanation: A ServeMux pattern with no method prefix, like the original "/items/{id}", matches that path for any HTTP method (GET, DELETE, POST, anything), so a DELETE was routed to a handler written only with GET in mind and ran the 'fetching item' logic for what should have been a different operation. The fix adds a method prefix, "GET /items/{id}", one of Go 1.22's ServeMux enhancements: the pattern now matches only GET (and HEAD) requests. A DELETE request to the same path no longer matches this registration. It would need its own "DELETE /items/{id}" registration to be handled. With only the GET pattern registered, ServeMux answers 405 Method Not Allowed (with an Allow header), because the path matches a pattern but the method does not; a path that matches nothing gets 404.

assessments.prompt: Why does http.HandleFunc accept a plain function of type func(http.ResponseWriter, *http.Request) directly, while http.Handle requires an argument that already satisfies http.Handler?
options: http.HandleFunc and http.Handle are actually interchangeable aliases for the exact same function with no real difference.
http.HandleFunc internally converts its function argument to the http.HandlerFunc type.
http.Handle only works with struct-based handlers, never with functions, due to a limitation in how interfaces are implemented in Go.
http.HandleFunc registers the route but never actually calls the provided function when a request arrives; it exists only for documentation purposes.
assessments.explanation: http.HandleFunc's entire purpose is to bridge the gap between 'I have a plain function with the right signature' and 'net/http needs something with a ServeHTTP method' -- it does this by wrapping the function argument in an http.HandlerFunc value before registering it, since http.HandlerFunc is a named function type with a ServeHTTP method defined on it that simply invokes the underlying function. http.Handle, by contrast, expects you to already be passing something typed as http.Handler, with no such wrapping performed for you -- passing a bare function to Handle would be a compile error unless you performed the http.HandlerFunc(...) conversion yourself first. The “http.HandleFunc and http.Handle are actually interchangeable aliases…” option is wrong -- they have genuinely different parameter types and behavior. The “http.Handle only works with struct-based handlers, never…” option is wrong -- Handle works perfectly well with any http.Handler, struct-based or otherwise; the distinction is about what conversion happens automatically, not what kinds of handlers are supported. The “http.HandleFunc registers the route but never actually…” option is wrong -- HandleFunc's registered function absolutely is called on matching requests, exactly like any other registered handler.

assessments.prompt: Calling `http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil)` starts a server using which handler, and what's a concrete risk of relying on this in a real service, according to this concept?
options: It requires that http.NewServeMux() has already been called at least once elsewhere in the program, or the call panics immediately.
It starts the server with no handler at all, so every request receives a 404, since nil is never a valid second argument in practice.

It uses http.DefaultServeMux, a single shared, package-level ServeMux that any package -- including third-party ones -- might register routes onto via the package-level http.HandleFunc, creating a real risk of unrelated code silently colliding on route registration.
It automatically creates and uses a brand-new, private http.NewServeMux() dedicated to that one ListenAndServe call, with no sharing risk of any kind.
assessments.explanation: Passing nil as the handler argument to ListenAndServe falls back to http.DefaultServeMux, a single mux shared at the package level -- the same instance that the package-level http.HandleFunc function (as opposed to a method on your own mux) registers routes onto. Because this mux is genuinely shared and globally accessible, any other code in the program, including a third-party dependency that itself calls http.HandleFunc, could register onto the exact same mux and silently collide with your own routes. The “It starts the server with no handler…” option is wrong -- nil is a valid and meaningful argument specifically triggering the default-mux fallback, not an error. The “It automatically creates and uses a brand-new…” option is wrong -- nothing new and private is created; DefaultServeMux is a pre-existing, shared package-level value. The “It requires that http.NewServeMux() has already been…” option is wrong -- DefaultServeMux always exists as soon as the net/http package is imported; there's no such precondition.

assessments.prompt: Given `mux.HandleFunc("GET /articles/{slug}", articleHandler)` and an incoming request to `/articles/go-basics?slug=other`, what does `r.PathValue("slug")` return inside articleHandler?
options: "other" -- PathValue and query parameters both read from the same underlying "slug" key, with the query string value taking precedence.
"go-basics?slug=other" -- PathValue returns the entire remainder of the URL, including the query string, as one combined value.
An error -- having a query parameter and a path wildcard both named "slug" on the same request is disallowed and rejected by net/http.
"go-basics" -- PathValue reads from the matched URL path segment, entirely independent of anything present in the query string.
assessments.explanation: r.PathValue("slug") retrieves whatever the named {slug} wildcard in the registered pattern actually matched against the request's URL path -- here, the path segment "go-basics" -- which is an entirely separate mechanism from query string parameters, retrieved instead via r.URL.Query(). There's no interaction, precedence rule, or naming conflict between the two just because they happen to share the name "slug"; they're read through completely different methods reading from completely different parts of the URL. The “"other" -- PathValue and query parameters both…” option invents a precedence rule that doesn't exist. The “"go-basics?slug=other" -- PathValue returns the entire remainder…” option misdescribes what PathValue returns -- it's just the one matched segment, not any larger portion of the URL. The “An error -- having a query parameter…” option invents a restriction net/http doesn't impose.

assessments.prompt: Which statement correctly describes when calling `w.Header().Set("X-Custom", "value")` inside a handler actually has an effect on what the client receives?
options: Only if it's called before the status line and headers have been sent.
At any point during the handler's execution, since Header() always mutates the live, already-transmitted header state directly.
Only if it's called after the first Write, since HTTP headers are physically appended to the end of the response body.
Only if WriteHeader is never explicitly called anywhere else in the handler, under any circumstances.
assessments.explanation: Header() returns a mutable map that you're free to modify before anything else locks the response in -- but the moment the status and headers are actually sent to the client (via an explicit WriteHeader call, or implicitly via the first Write), that header state is committed and transmitted; later Header() mutations simply modify a map that has no further effect on what the client already received. The “At any point during the handler's execution…” option is wrong -- headers aren't 'live' in that sense; once sent, they're sent. The “Only if it's called after the first…” option inverts HTTP's actual structure -- headers precede the body, not the reverse, and Header() mutations must happen before any body bytes go out. The “Only if WriteHeader is never explicitly called…” option is wrong -- what matters is the relative order of the Header() call versus whenever the status/headers actually get sent, not merely whether WriteHeader happens to be called explicitly at all elsewhere.

assessments.prompt: Explain how net/http's Handler interface and HandlerFunc adapter reflect the same 'small interfaces over large frameworks' philosophy introduced with io.Reader, and why that design choice matters specifically for the middleware pattern covered later in this module.
assessments.modelAnswer: http.Handler is deliberately as small as an interface can be -- a single method, ServeHTTP(ResponseWriter, *Request), with no required base class, no lifecycle methods to override, and no explicit declaration tying a given type to the interface. Just like io.Reader's single Read method lets an enormous range of unrelated types (files, network connections, in-memory buffers) all work with generic code like io.Copy without any of them needing to know io.Reader exists, http.Handler's single method lets anything -- a plain function wrapped via HandlerFunc, a struct carrying its own configuration and a ServeHTTP method, a router, a caching layer -- be treated identically by anything that only needs to call ServeHTTP on it, including net/http's own server loop, which has no idea what concrete type it's actually holding. HandlerFunc's role is to make this small interface friction-free for the extremely common case where a handler doesn't need to carry any state at all: rather than requiring every handler author to define a named struct type and a method just to satisfy one interface, HandlerFunc lets a plain function value be converted, with a single explicit conversion, into something that already has the required ServeHTTP method built in by the standard library. This matters enormously for middleware, covered later in this module, because middleware in Go is fundamentally a function that accepts a Handler and returns a new Handler wrapping it -- and because Handler is such a minimal, uniform interface, a middleware function doesn't need to know or care whether the Handler it's wrapping is a plain HandlerFunc-adapted function, a struct-based handler, or even another layer of middleware wrapping something else underneath; it only ever needs to call that one ServeHTTP method (or, more commonly at the source level, the equivalent) on whatever it was handed. If Handler required multiple methods, or if handlers needed to inherit from some base implementation, composing arbitrary chains of middleware around arbitrary handlers -- the entire mechanism the next concept explores -- would be dramatically more constrained and far less uniform than it is.

concepts.title: Encoding and Decoding JSON
concepts.description: encoding/json's Decoder and Encoder types stream JSON directly to and from an io.Reader/io.Writer -- exactly the kind of composition small interfaces enable -- and struct tags control precisely how Go field names map onto JSON keys, which matters enormously once you're reading untrusted request bodies and writing response bodies for real clients.
learningObjectives: Decode a JSON request body into a Go struct using json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode, and explain why streaming decode is preferable to reading the whole body into memory first.
Use struct tags (json:"name", omitempty, json:"-") to control which fields are included in encoded JSON and under what key names.
Encode a Go value to a JSON response with json.NewEncoder(w).Encode, and set the Content-Type header before writing any body content.
Distinguish the different kinds of decode errors (malformed syntax, wrong value type, empty body) and respond with an appropriate HTTP status code for each rather than a generic failure.
Explain what happens to unexported struct fields and to JSON fields with no matching struct field during decode and encode.

sections.heading: Decoding a Request Body: Decoder Over a Reader, Not Unmarshal Over Bytes
Struct Tags: Field Names, omitempty, and Exported-Only Visibility
sections.body:
By default, encoding/json includes every **exported** field of a struct, using the Go field name as the JSON key: `Name string` becomes `"Name": ...` with no tag needed. A `json:"..."` struct tag lets you override that default in three common ways:

```go
type User struct {
	Name     string `json:"name"`              // renames the JSON key to lowercase "name"
	Nickname string `json:"nickname,omitempty"`  // omitted from output entirely if Nickname == ""
	password string `json:"-"`                   // unexported anyway -- always excluded, tag or not
	Internal string `json:"-"`                   // exported, but explicitly excluded via "-"
}
```

`omitempty` drops the field from the output when its value is the zero value for its type (empty string, 0, nil, false, an empty slice or map), which suits optional fields where you'd rather the client see no key than an explicit `null` or `0`. `json:"-"` excludes a field from both encoding and decoding regardless of its value, the standard way to keep an exported field internal-only.

This reuses the exported/unexported rule from the Packages concept: **unexported fields (lowercase first letter) are always excluded from JSON encoding and decoding, and no tag can opt them back in.** encoding/json is ordinary reflection-based code in another package, so it cannot see or set them. A frequent beginner mistake is defining a request struct with lowercase field names, expecting the tags to include them, and finding every field empty after decoding: the tag on an unexported field does nothing, because the field was never reachable.

sections.heading: Encoding a Response, and the Header-Before-Body Rule Again
Handling Decode Errors as Distinct, Actionable Cases
sections.body:
A `Decode` call can fail for different reasons, and collapsing them into one generic 'bad request' response (or, worse, ignoring the error and proceeding with a zero-valued struct) throws away information a client could use to fix the request:

- **Malformed JSON syntax** (a trailing comma, unquoted keys) returns a `*json.SyntaxError`. A body cut off mid-document returns `io.ErrUnexpectedEOF` instead.
- **A JSON value that doesn't match the target field's Go type**, such as a string where the struct expects a number, returns a `*json.UnmarshalTypeError`, which also names the field and offset.
- **An empty request body** returns `io.EOF`. That is distinct from a syntax error and usually means the client forgot to send a body.

```go
var req CreateUserRequest
err := json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&req)
switch {
case errors.Is(err, io.EOF):
	http.Error(w, "request body is empty", http.StatusBadRequest)
	return
case err != nil:
	http.Error(w, fmt.Sprintf("invalid JSON: %v", err), http.StatusBadRequest)
	return
}
```

All of these warrant a `4xx` status, since they're the client's fault, but telling them apart, even only in the message text, gives a client-side developer something to act on. Note what `Decode` does **not** treat as an error by default: JSON fields with no matching struct field are ignored (keys are matched case-insensitively against field names or tags, and dropped if nothing matches). Unless you call `DisallowUnknownFields()` on the decoder, a missing tag or an unexpected extra field will not make `Decode` fail.

examples.title: Decoding a Request Body Into a Struct
examples.explanation: `json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&req)` reads from the request body into `req`, filling `Name` and `Age` from the JSON keys that match their tags (`"name"` and `"age"`). Note the order in the success path: `w.WriteHeader(http.StatusCreated)` is called before `Encode` can implicitly send `200 OK` with its first write. This is the pattern for any handler that needs a non-200 success status (201 Created is conventional for creating a resource) alongside a JSON body. `Content-Type` is set before `WriteHeader`, which comes before `Encode`'s first byte, so every header change happens before anything locks the response in.

examples.title: Struct Tags in Action: omitempty and Unexported Fields
examples.explanation: `Nickname` is in the struct but omitted from the output, because it's tagged `omitempty` and its value is the empty string, the zero value for `string`. `password`, despite carrying a `json:"password"` tag that looks like it should include it under the key `"password"`, is never included at all (`go vet` flags a json tag on an unexported field for exactly this reason) -- because `password` starts with a lowercase letter it's unexported, and encoding/json (reflection with no special access) cannot read it, so the tag is inert. This is a common trap: reading only the tags, you might assume `password` is serialized under `"password"`, when it will never appear in the output whatever it holds. The capitalization of the field name, not the tag, decides visibility.

examples.title: Distinguishing Decode Error Cases
examples.code:
package main

import (
	"encoding/json"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"net/http"
)

type Order struct {
	Quantity int `json:"quantity"`
}

func createOrderHandler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	var order Order
	err := json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&order)

	var typeErr *json.UnmarshalTypeError
	switch {
	case errors.Is(err, io.EOF):
		http.Error(w, "request body must not be empty", http.StatusBadRequest)
		return
	case errors.As(err, &typeErr):
		http.Error(w, fmt.Sprintf("field %q must be a %s", typeErr.Field, typeErr.Type), http.StatusBadRequest)
		return
	case err != nil:
		http.Error(w, "malformed JSON in request body", http.StatusBadRequest)
		return
	}

	w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
	json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(order)
}
examples.explanation: `errors.Is(err, io.EOF)` catches an empty body and tells the client what is wrong (nothing was sent) rather than reporting a parse failure. `errors.As(err, &typeErr)` checks for a `*json.UnmarshalTypeError`: if the client sent `{"quantity": "five"}`, this branch fires and reports the field and expected type from information the error carries. Any other non-nil error, most often malformed syntax, falls through to a generic 'malformed JSON' message. All three branches return 400 Bad Request, but the message text differs, which gives whoever debugs the client integration a starting point.

misconceptions.description: A struct field needs a json tag in order to be included in the output when the struct is marshaled to JSON -- without one, encoding/json has no way to know what to do with it.
misconceptions.clarification: Exported fields are included in marshaled JSON by default, using the Go field name as the JSON key, with no tag required. A json tag is only needed to change that default: renaming the key, adding omitempty, or excluding the field with "-". Whether a field can be included at all depends on whether it's exported (capitalized): unexported fields are always excluded, tag or not.
misconceptions.fact: Exported fields are included in marshaled JSON by default, using the Go field's own name verbatim as the JSON key, with no tag required at all.

misconceptions.description: Any error returned from json.Decode means the client sent an empty or disconnected request, so it's safe to treat every decode error identically with one generic error response.
misconceptions.clarification: Decode can fail for several different reasons: an empty body (io.EOF), malformed JSON (a *json.SyntaxError), or a value whose JSON type doesn't match the target Go field (a *json.UnmarshalTypeError, which names the offending field). Collapsing all of these into one generic message discards information the error already carries, and passing it back to the caller would help them fix the request faster.

exercises.prompt: Given this struct and this value, what exact JSON string does json.Marshal produce?
exercises.code:
type Item struct {
	Title       string `json:"title"`
	Description string `json:"description,omitempty"`
	Quantity    int    `json:"quantity,omitempty"`
	internalID  string `json:"internal_id"`
}

item := Item{
	Title:       "Widget",
	Description: "",
	Quantity:    0,
	internalID:  "abc-123",
}
data, _ := json.Marshal(item)
fmt.Println(string(data))
hints: Title has no omitempty and a non-zero value, so it's always included under its tagged key.
Description and Quantity are both tagged omitempty and both currently hold their zero values ("" and 0) -- what does omitempty do to a field in exactly that state?
internalID starts with a lowercase letter -- does its json tag matter at all, regardless of what value it holds?
exercises.expectedAnswer: {"title":"Widget"} -- Description and Quantity are both omitted because they're tagged omitempty and hold their zero values. internalID is omitted entirely because it's unexported (lowercase), regardless of its json tag or its non-empty value "abc-123" -- encoding/json cannot see unexported fields at all.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Title is exported, has no omitempty, and holds "Widget", so it's included as "title". Description is tagged omitempty and holds "" (the zero value for string), so it's dropped. Quantity is tagged omitempty and holds 0, so it's dropped too. internalID starts with a lowercase letter, so it's unexported; encoding/json cannot read unexported fields, so its json:"internal_id" tag is inert and it never appears in the output. The marshaled result contains only the field that is exported and either lacks omitempty or holds a non-zero value: {"title":"Widget"}.

exercises.prompt: This handler is supposed to return a JSON response with the correct Content-Type header, but clients report receiving a response with no Content-Type header set at all (or an incorrect default one, depending on the client). Find and fix the bug.
hints: Look at the order of the two lines: which one actually sends bytes to the client first?
Encode writes body bytes, and if no status/headers have been sent yet, that first write implicitly locks in the response's headers (with a default Content-Type) right then and there.
Once headers are sent, a later call to w.Header().Set(...) modifies a header map that has already been flushed -- it has no effect on what the client receives. Reorder the two lines.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original code calls Encode first, whose first internal Write sends the response headers immediately, because nothing had been sent yet. It uses whatever Content-Type was in the header map at that moment (none, since the Set call hadn't run). The later w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json") modifies the map after the headers have gone out, so it has no effect on the response. When no Content-Type has been set, net/http sniffs one from the first bytes written, which for JSON text gives text/plain; charset=utf-8. The fix reorders the two lines: set Content-Type first, so it's in the header map when Encode's first Write triggers the implicit header send, then call Encode.

assessments.prompt: A struct field is declared as `Count int` with no json tag at all. What happens when a value of that struct is marshaled to JSON?
options: The field is included, but only if its value is non-zero -- untagged fields behave as if they had an implicit omitempty.
The field is silently omitted, since only tagged fields are ever included in JSON output.
Marshaling fails with an error, since encoding/json requires every field to have an explicit tag.
The field is included in the output using the exact Go field name, "Count", as the JSON key, since exported fields are included by default with no tag required.
assessments.explanation: Exported fields (capitalized, like Count) are included in marshaled JSON by default, using the Go field name as the JSON key, with no tag required. A tag is only needed to change that default (rename the key, add omitempty, or exclude the field with "-"). The “The field is silently omitted, since only…” and “Marshaling fails with an error, since encoding/json…” options are both wrong because they assume a tag is required for inclusion at all, which is backwards -- untagged exported fields are included, not excluded or erroring. The “The field is included, but only…” option is wrong -- there is no implicit omitempty behavior for untagged fields; a zero-value untagged field is still included in the output (e.g. "Count":0), which is precisely why omitempty has to be added explicitly whenever that default inclusion-of-zero-values isn't wanted.

assessments.prompt: What is the concrete practical difference between calling json.Unmarshal(data, &v) and calling json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&v) when handling an HTTP request body?
options: Unmarshal is strictly faster in every situation, since Decode carries extra overhead purely from satisfying the io.Reader interface.

Unmarshal requires the entire JSON payload already buffered in memory as a []byte (typically obtained via io.ReadAll(r.Body) first), while Decode reads and parses directly from r.Body as an io.Reader, streaming through the input incrementally rather than requiring it all up front.
There is no real functional difference between the two -- both necessarily read the entire body into memory before any parsing can begin.
Decode can only ever be used with an *http.Request's body specifically, while Unmarshal works with byte slices from any source at all.
assessments.explanation: Unmarshal needs a []byte already in hand, which for an HTTP body means an io.ReadAll call and a full read pass before Unmarshal starts; Decode reads from any io.Reader (r.Body is one) and parses as bytes arrive, without buffering the whole payload first. The “Unmarshal is strictly faster in every situation…” option invents a performance claim the material never makes; if anything, avoiding the extra buffering step is the practical advantage described. The “Decode can only ever be used…” option is wrong -- Decode works with any io.Reader, not exclusively request bodies; r.Body is simply a common, convenient example. The “There is no real functional difference between…” option is wrong -- this is precisely the distinction the concept draws; Decode's whole advantage is not needing the full body in memory first.

assessments.prompt: A struct declares an exported field: `InternalNotes string` tagged `json:"-"`. What happens to this field when a value of the struct is marshaled to JSON?
options: It's unconditionally excluded from the encoded JSON regardless of its value.
It's included in the output under the literal JSON key "-", since that's exactly what the tag specifies.
It's included using the Go field name "InternalNotes" as the key, because a tag value of "-" is invalid and therefore silently ignored.
json.Marshal returns an error for this struct, since "-" can never be used as a JSON key.
assessments.explanation: The json:"-" tag means 'exclude this field from encoding and decoding,' whatever value it holds. It's the standard way to keep an exported field out of the JSON. The “It's included in the output under…” option misreads "-" as an ordinary literal key name rather than the special exclusion marker it actually is. The “It's included using the Go field name…” option wrongly assumes the tag is invalid syntax; it's a valid and specifically meaningful tag value. The “json.Marshal returns an error for this struct…” option is wrong -- this doesn't produce a marshal error; the field is simply, silently omitted from the result.

assessments.prompt: A client sends `{"name": "Amy", "age": 30, "extra_field": "surprise"}` to an endpoint whose target struct only defines Name and Age fields -- nothing corresponding to extra_field exists anywhere on the struct. What happens by default when this is decoded with json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&req)?
options: Decode succeeds, and Go automatically adds a new field to the struct at runtime to hold extra_field's value.
Decode returns an error immediately, because extra_field has no corresponding field on the target struct.
Decode succeeds with no error at all; extra_field is silently ignored and dropped.
Decode succeeds only if the struct happens to have a field literally named ExtraField somewhere, matched case-insensitively.
assessments.explanation: By default, JSON keys are matched case-insensitively against struct field names or tags and dropped if nothing matches, which does not make Decode fail. Rejecting unknown fields is opt-in: call DisallowUnknownFields() on the decoder before Decode. Without that, an extra field like extra_field is ignored. The “Decode returns an error immediately, because extra_field…” and “Decode succeeds only if the struct happens…” options both wrongly assume rejection or a matching requirement is the default behavior. The “Decode succeeds, and Go automatically adds…” option invents a runtime struct-mutation capability Go does not have -- struct shape is fixed at compile time.

assessments.prompt: Walk through everything that can go wrong when decoding a JSON request body in an HTTP handler, and explain how to respond appropriately to each distinct case rather than collapsing them into one generic error response.
assessments.modelAnswer: A call to json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&target) can fail in at least three different ways, and each deserves its own handling rather than one 'bad request' response. First, the body might be empty, which Decode reports as io.EOF; checking errors.Is(err, io.EOF) lets you say a body was expected but none arrived, rather than implying their JSON was malformed. Second, the body might contain invalid JSON (a trailing comma, an unquoted key), which surfaces as a *json.SyntaxError; reporting it as a parse failure, optionally with the error's message naming the byte offset, gives the client developer something to check. (A body cut off mid-document gives io.ErrUnexpectedEOF instead.) Third, the JSON might be valid but hold a value of the wrong type for the target field, such as a string where a number belongs, which produces a *json.UnmarshalTypeError; that error names the offending field and the expected type, which is worth surfacing in the response. All three warrant a 4xx status, typically 400 Bad Request, since the fault is the client's; the distinction that matters is in the message. Remember what does NOT produce a decode error by default: extra fields the struct doesn't define are ignored unless you configure the decoder with DisallowUnknownFields, so a handler that must reject them has to opt in.

concepts.title: The Middleware Pattern
concepts.description: Middleware in Go is simply a function that accepts an http.Handler and returns a new http.Handler wrapping it -- a direct, practical payoff of the small-interface Handler design that lets logging, authentication, and other cross-cutting concerns be composed around a handler without that handler ever needing to know they exist.
learningObjectives: Explain what the middleware pattern is and why it separates cross-cutting concerns like logging and authentication from a handler's own business logic.
Write a middleware function with signature func(http.Handler) http.Handler that wraps a handler with logging behavior around the call to the wrapped handler.
Chain multiple middleware functions together in a deliberate order, and explain how that order changes observable behavior.
Use context.Context with an unexported key type to pass a request-scoped value (such as an authenticated user) from middleware into a downstream handler safely.
Explain why middleware that rejects a request (such as failed authentication) must return immediately after writing its response, rather than falling through to call the wrapped handler.

sections.heading: What Middleware Is, and Why It Exists
sections.body:
Real HTTP services need the same few behaviors around nearly every request: logging it, checking that the caller is authenticated, recovering from a panic so one bad request doesn't take down the server, timing it. Writing all of that inside every handler duplicates it and ties unrelated concerns (is this user allowed to do this? what does this endpoint do?) together in one function body, making both harder to read, test, and change.

**Middleware** solves this by wrapping a handler in another handler that runs some behavior, calls the original, and optionally runs more behavior afterward, without the original handler knowing it's wrapped:

```go
type Middleware func(http.Handler) http.Handler
```

A middleware is a function that takes an `http.Handler` (the "next" handler in the chain) and returns a new `http.Handler` that wraps it. This works cleanly because `http.Handler` has exactly one method, so "wrap a Handler" only means "produce something else with that one method," however many layers deep or whatever type sits at the center.

sections.heading: Writing a Logging Middleware
Chaining Middleware, and Why Order Changes Behavior
Passing Values Downstream Safely With context.Context
The Critical `return`: Why Falling Through After a Rejection Is a Common Bug

examples.title: A Standalone Logging Middleware
examples.explanation: `LoggingMiddleware(mux)` wraps the whole mux, not one route, in a single logging layer. Wrapping the mux logs every route uniformly in one place, instead of each `HandleFunc` call opting in separately. `wrapped` is an `http.Handler` (the `http.HandlerFunc` that `LoggingMiddleware` returned) and goes to `http.ListenAndServe` where `mux` itself would have gone. `ListenAndServe` cannot tell a bare mux from a mux wrapped in any number of middleware layers, which is the point of the pattern.

examples.title: Chaining Multiple Middleware in a Chosen Order
examples.explanation: `Chain` applies its middlewares in reverse (`mws[len(mws)-1]` first) so that the call order matches the order they are *listed* at the call site. `Chain(mux, RecoverMiddleware, LoggingMiddleware, AuthMiddleware)` gives a handler where `RecoverMiddleware` is outermost (first to see every request, including ones that later panic), `LoggingMiddleware` is next (logging every request that gets this far, including ones Auth will reject), and `AuthMiddleware` is innermost, just before the mux. Putting `RecoverMiddleware` outermost is the usual convention: only a layer that wraps *everything* below it can catch a panic from an inner middleware or handler with a deferred `recover()` and turn it into a 500. (`net/http` already recovers panics per connection, but only to log them and close the connection.)

examples.title: Auth Middleware Passing a User via context.Context
examples.explanation: The unexported `contextKey` type and its constant `userContextKey` keep this key from colliding with a key from any other package, even one that stores its value under a plain string like "user" or an int with the same value: Go treats `contextKey(0)` as a different type from a bare `int` or `string`, so only code in this package can produce a matching key. The `return` after `http.Error` is what enforces the auth check; without it `next.ServeHTTP` would run whether or not `ok` was true. `profileHandler` reads the user with the comma-ok form, `user, _ := r.Context().Value(userContextKey).(User)`, which yields a zero `User` instead of panicking if the middleware was not in the chain. The single-value form would panic in that case.

misconceptions.description: Using a plain string like "user" as the key argument to context.WithValue and context.Value is a harmless, common convenience, since context keys are just meant to be simple lookup labels.
misconceptions.clarification: A plain string (or any built-in type like int) used directly as a context key risks collisions across unrelated packages: any other code, including a third-party middleware you don't control, could use the same string, and the two would read and overwrite each other's value with no compiler warning, because context values are distinguished only by the key's type and value together. The idiomatic fix is a small unexported named type in your own package (commonly int-based) and a constant of that type as the key. No other package can construct a value of that type, so the key can't collide with theirs, whatever underlying value either uses.

misconceptions.description: If a middleware writes an error status and message to the ResponseWriter (for example via http.Error) inside an if block, execution automatically stops there -- there's no need to add an explicit return statement afterward.
misconceptions.clarification: Writing to an http.ResponseWriter is an ordinary function call with no effect on control flow: it does not make the function return or stop executing later statements. Without a `return` right after the error response, execution falls through to whatever comes next, which in middleware is usually next.ServeHTTP(w, r), so the wrapped handler runs even for a request that should have been rejected. The bug is easy to introduce because the code compiles without warning and passes casual testing whenever only the happy path (successful auth) is tried.
misconceptions.fact: Writing to an http.ResponseWriter is an ordinary function call with no special control-flow effect on the surrounding Go code -- it does not cause the function to return, panic, or otherwise stop executing subsequent statements.

exercises.prompt: Given this middleware chain and handler, in what exact order do the four print statements execute when a single request comes in?
hints: Read the wrapping from the outside in to find the order execution ENTERS each layer: MiddlewareA wraps MiddlewareB, which wraps finalHandler.
Each middleware's 'before' print happens before it calls next.ServeHTTP, and its 'after' print happens once next.ServeHTTP has fully returned.
Think of it like nested parentheses or an onion: the outermost layer's 'before' runs first, and its 'after' runs LAST, once everything inside it has completely finished.
exercises.expectedAnswer: A: before, B: before, final handler, B: after, A: after -- in that exact order. Execution enters the outermost middleware (A) first, then the next layer in (B), then the innermost handler, and then unwinds back out in the reverse order, with each layer's 'after' print firing only once everything it wrapped has fully completed.
exercises.solutionExplanation: handler is MiddlewareA wrapping (MiddlewareB wrapping finalHandler), so handler.ServeHTTP first runs MiddlewareA's body: it prints 'A: before' and calls next.ServeHTTP, which is MiddlewareB's. That prints 'B: before' and calls its next.ServeHTTP, which is finalHandler: it prints 'final handler' and returns. Control returns into MiddlewareB, past its next.ServeHTTP call, which prints 'B: after'; then into MiddlewareA, which prints 'A: after' and returns to the caller. The 'before' prints run outside-to-inside and the 'after' prints inside-to-outside, as with nested function calls.

exercises.prompt: This auth middleware is supposed to block any request without a valid API key, responding with 401 and never running the wrapped handler for rejected requests. Instead, testers report that even requests with a missing or wrong API key still seem to trigger the wrapped handler's real behavior (visible via its own log lines), alongside the 401 response. Find and fix the bug.
hints: Writing to the ResponseWriter with http.Error does not, by itself, stop the enclosing function from continuing to its next statement.
Trace execution when key != validAPIKey is true: http.Error runs, and then what's the very next line the function executes?
Add an explicit return statement immediately after the http.Error call, inside the if block, so next.ServeHTTP is never reached for a rejected request.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original code writes a 401 with http.Error when the key check fails but has no return inside the if block, so whether or not the key was valid, execution reaches the unconditional next.ServeHTTP(w, r) below it. A rejected request therefore still runs the wrapped handler (which is why its log lines appear for invalid keys) after the 401 has been sent, and if that handler writes its own status you also get a 'superfluous response.WriteHeader call' warning, on top of the security bug of running privileged logic for an unauthenticated request. Adding `return` right after http.Error makes the function exit when the check fails, so next.ServeHTTP is never reached for a rejected request.

assessments.prompt: Given `handler := LoggingMiddleware(AuthMiddleware(finalHandler))`, which statement correctly describes the order requests and responses flow through these three pieces?
options: LoggingMiddleware and AuthMiddleware both run before the request even reaches finalHandler, but which of the two runs first is undefined and decided randomly by the Go runtime.
Requests flow LoggingMiddleware -> AuthMiddleware -> finalHandler; the response then unwinds back through AuthMiddleware and LoggingMiddleware in reverse.
All three run simultaneously in separate goroutines, so there is no defined ordering between them.
Requests flow finalHandler -> AuthMiddleware -> LoggingMiddleware, and responses flow back in the same order.
assessments.explanation: LoggingMiddleware is the outermost wrapper, so its body starts first when a request arrives; it calls AuthMiddleware, which calls finalHandler if authentication succeeds. When finalHandler returns, control unwinds through AuthMiddleware's remaining code and then LoggingMiddleware's (its timing log), so that log line includes the time spent in everything nested inside it. The “Requests flow finalHandler -> AuthMiddleware -> LoggingMiddleware…” option describes the reverse order, which is wrong. The “All three run simultaneously in separate goroutines…” option is wrong -- middleware wrapping is synchronous, sequential function calls, not concurrent goroutines, unless a middleware explicitly spawns one itself. The “LoggingMiddleware and AuthMiddleware both run before…” option is wrong -- the order is entirely deterministic and directly determined by the nesting shown in the wrapping expression itself, not randomized.

assessments.prompt: Two independently-developed middleware functions both call context.WithValue using the plain string "user" as the key. What's the concrete risk this creates, and what's the idiomatic fix?
options: The two middleware's stored values can silently collide -- one overwrites or is misread as the other's, with no compile-time warning -- because context distinguishes values only by key type and value together, and two identical strings are indistinguishable; the idiomatic fix is for each package to define its own small, unexported named type and use a constant of that type as its key, since no other package can construct a colliding value of a type it doesn't define.
This is only a risk if both middleware happen to run in the same goroutine; running them in separate goroutines eliminates the collision risk entirely.
This triggers a runtime panic the moment the second WithValue call executes, since context.Context enforces globally unique string keys across the whole program.
No real risk -- context.Context automatically namespaces stored values by which package called WithValue, so identical string keys from different packages can never actually collide.
assessments.explanation: context.Context has no per-package namespacing: two WithValue calls using the string "user" as the key are indistinguishable to the context, so a later Value("user") lookup can return the wrong package's data, with nothing at compile time to warn you. The fix is the unexported-type-as-key idiom: no other package can construct a value of a type it doesn't define, so a key of such a type can't collide with another package's key, whatever underlying value either uses. The “No real risk -- context.Context automatically namespaces…” option invents an automatic namespacing mechanism context.Context doesn't have. The “This triggers a runtime panic the moment…” option invents a uniqueness-enforcement panic that doesn't exist. The “This is only a risk if both…” option is wrong -- this is a data-collision issue tied to the key's identity, entirely unrelated to which goroutine either call happens to run in.

assessments.prompt: The Chain helper function iterates over its middlewares slice in reverse (`for i := len(mws) - 1; i >= 0; i--`) while building the wrapped handler. Why, according to this concept?
options: Reverse iteration is required because Go slices cannot be safely traversed forward inside a for loop when their contents are being reassigned.
It causes every middleware in the slice to run concurrently instead of sequentially, one per goroutine.
Iterating in reverse is purely an arbitrary implementation detail with no effect on the resulting handler's actual behavior.

It's specifically so the resulting call order matches the order middlewares are listed at the call site -- applying the last-listed middleware first (making it the innermost wrap) and the first-listed middleware last (making it the outermost wrap) ensures the first middleware named in the list is the first one to actually run when a request arrives.
assessments.explanation: Wrapping happens from the inside out: the middleware applied last in the loop ends up outermost, since each wrap sits around everything built so far. By walking the slice from the end, Chain wraps mws[0], the first one listed, last, so it is the outermost layer and the first to run on an incoming request. That is what lets the call-site order (Chain(finalHandler, LoggingMiddleware, AuthMiddleware)) read as the execution order. The “Iterating in reverse is purely an arbitrary…” option understates a genuine, deliberate mechanism. The “Reverse iteration is required because Go slices…” option invents a slice-safety constraint that doesn't apply here. The “It causes every middleware in the slice…” option misdescribes what the loop does -- it's ordinary sequential wrapping, not concurrent execution.

assessments.prompt: In `Chain(mux, RecoverMiddleware, LoggingMiddleware, AuthMiddleware)`, RecoverMiddleware is deliberately listed first, making it the outermost wrapper around everything else. Why, according to this concept?
options: Placement within the list has no real effect on what RecoverMiddleware is able to catch -- any position in the chain would behave identically.
Placing RecoverMiddleware outermost causes it to run in a separate goroutine from the rest of the chain, isolating any panics automatically without an explicit recover() call.
Only the outermost layer, wrapping everything beneath it, can reliably catch a panic occurring anywhere in the inner layers or the final handler via a deferred recover() call.
RecoverMiddleware is required by net/http itself to run innermost, immediately wrapping the final handler, or the program fails to compile.
assessments.explanation: A deferred recover() in a middleware layer can only catch a panic raised inside that same call, which for RecoverMiddleware means everything it wraps. Placed outermost, that covers every other middleware and the final handler, so a panic anywhere in the chain is caught and turned into a clean response. If it sat further in, a panic in a layer wrapping it from outside (such as LoggingMiddleware) would pass it by. The “Placement within the list has no real…” option directly contradicts this positional dependency. The “RecoverMiddleware is required by net/http itself…” option invents a net/http-level requirement that doesn't exist -- middleware ordering is entirely up to the developer. The “Placing RecoverMiddleware outermost causes it to run…” option invents a goroutine-isolation behavior that recover()/middleware wrapping doesn't provide on its own.

assessments.prompt: Explain the middleware pattern to a developer who understands http.Handler but has never written or read middleware before, and explain specifically why forgetting a return statement after a short-circuiting error response is such a common and dangerous mistake in this pattern.
assessments.modelAnswer: Middleware is a function that takes an http.Handler and returns a new http.Handler that wraps it: it runs some behavior, calls the wrapped handler's ServeHTTP, and optionally runs more behavior once that call returns. This works cleanly because http.Handler has one method, so 'wrap a handler' just means 'produce another thing with that ServeHTTP method.' Middleware can be stacked arbitrarily deep, and neither the mux that registers the result nor any layer needs to know how many layers there are or what the innermost handler does. That separates cross-cutting concerns (logging, authentication, panic recovery) from each handler's business logic: the handler stays focused on its job, and behavior that applies to many handlers is written once as a wrapping layer. The return-statement danger is specific to middleware that's meant to short-circuit a request -- reject it outright, most commonly for failed authentication -- before it ever reaches the wrapped handler. Writing an error response with http.Error(w, ...) is an ordinary function call with no effect on the enclosing function's control flow, so unless it is immediately followed by a return, execution continues to the next statement, which in nearly every middleware is the unconditional next.ServeHTTP(w, r). Forgetting the return means the middleware writes its rejection and then runs the wrapped handler anyway, whether or not the check passed. It is dangerous because it is easy to miss: the code compiles, a request that passes the check behaves the same with or without the return, and the bug shows only on a request that should have been rejected, the unhappy path a developer is least likely to test.
